title: Ireland’s AI opportunity is distributed through existing differences in work exposure, gender, skills, ownership and worker voice
source_unit: TASC, AI and Inequality: Spotlight on the Key Issues Affecting Ireland, part of The State We Are In: Inequality in Ireland 2026
geography: Ireland; workers, firms, communities and public institutions in a highly digitalised economy

observations.period: 2025-2026; Ireland’s digital economy and broad AI exposure

denominator.unit: TASC issue brief and cited Irish, EU and international sources

job_exposure.unit: per cent of Irish jobs estimated to be exposed to AI to some degree

digital_skills.unit: per cent of people ages 16-74 with at least basic digital skills in 2025

business_adoption.unit: per cent of Irish businesses reporting AI use in 2025, compared with 8.0% in 2023

distribution_question.value: The brief argues that adoption and skills are insufficient measures of inclusion unless ownership, control, distribution of productivity gains and worker/community voice are also addressed.

observations.method: Think-tank issue brief synthesising Irish government, EU, academic and international evidence; it is not a new representative survey or administrative dataset.
observations.uncertainty: Job exposure is not job loss, business adoption is not effective use, and digital skills do not establish equal access to AI benefits, bargaining power or public-service outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Irish workers, businesses and communities with different digital skills, occupations, resources and institutional access.
observations.counterinterpretation: High digital skills and technology-sector concentration may give Ireland stronger capacity to capture AI gains than many countries, even if distribution remains unequal.

observations.period: 2026; occupational exposure, complementarity and gendered distribution of AI risk

denominator.unit: TASC brief drawing on Department of Finance and labour-market analysis

benefit_position.unit: per cent of Irish roles described as positioned to benefit from AI-enabled productivity improvements

displacement_risk.unit: per cent of Irish jobs described as facing comparatively higher displacement risk

sector_exposure.value: Financial services and insurance were reported at 97% exposure and information and communication technology at 94% exposure.

gender_gap.value: 76% of women versus 51% of men were described as working in high-AI-exposure occupations; 38% of women versus 23% of men were in high-exposure, low-complementarity roles.

observations.method: Secondary analysis of occupational exposure and complementarity estimates cited by TASC, with sector, geography, gender, education and age comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: Exposure and complementarity classifications are model-based and do not directly observe adoption, layoffs, wage change, productivity, worker control or realized gender inequality.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, high- and low-complementarity occupations, financial/insurance and ICT workers, urban and rural labour markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: High exposure can mean augmentation rather than displacement; some high-exposure professional workers may gain productivity and time even while facing new performance or surveillance pressures.

observations.period: 2026; algorithmic management, recruitment, digital access and unequal participation

denominator.unit: TASC issue brief and cited labour, digital-inclusion and equality research

algorithmic_management.value: The brief cites EU evidence that about one in four workers report algorithmic management and about one-third use AI-powered tools; in Ireland, reported assignment of working time was 30% and assignment of tasks 26%.

digital_exclusion.value: Older adults, people with lower education and disadvantaged communities are described as less likely to have the skills, devices or connectivity needed to use AI safely and effectively.

automated_bias.value: The brief identifies risks from biased recruitment, facial recognition, inaccessible design, privacy loss, stereotype reproduction and synthetic sexual abuse, with disproportionate effects for women, darker-skinned people, LGBTQ+ people, children and disabled people.

voice_endpoint.value: Digital literacy, worker participation, collective bargaining, enforcement and accountability are presented as necessary complements to training and adoption.

observations.method: Literature and policy synthesis across labour, equality, accessibility, privacy and digital-governance sources; not an Irish longitudinal worker panel.
observations.uncertainty: The cited estimates use different populations, definitions and field periods; the brief does not estimate a single causal effect of AI on participation, safety or employment.
observations.subgroup: Older adults, lower-education and disadvantaged communities, women, disabled people, LGBTQ+ people, children, darker-skinned people and workers under algorithmic management.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can improve accessibility, translation, communication and independence for some people with disabilities and can support higher-value work; inclusion depends on design, access, privacy and remedy.

observations.period: 2026; AI governance, infrastructure dependency and distribution of social/environmental costs

denominator.unit: TASC issue brief and cited Irish, European and global policy sources

governance_orientation.value: The brief characterises Irish AI policy as strongly oriented toward adoption, investment, competitiveness and regulatory compliance, with less attention to redistribution of wealth, power and opportunity.

institutional_model.value: Ireland’s 2026 AI governance framework is described as distributed across 15 existing public bodies, overseen by an AI Office, rather than concentrated in a single regulator.

global_externalisation.value: The brief links AI value capture in advanced economies to critical-mineral extraction, data-labelling and content-moderation labour, and electronic-waste burdens in the Global South.

success_test.value: It argues AI success should be judged by fairness, inclusion, democratic participation and sustainability as well as technical performance, productivity and adoption.

observations.method: Normative and empirical policy analysis by an independent Irish think tank, using cited government, academic, civil-society and international sources.
observations.uncertainty: The governance critique is an interpretive assessment, and the brief does not measure the future distribution of AI gains or quantify Ireland’s causal contribution to global supply-chain harms.
observations.subgroup: Irish workers, communities, regulators and firms, plus workers and communities in global AI supply chains.
observations.counterinterpretation: Competitiveness-led AI investment can expand public revenue, jobs and service capacity; the distributional question is whether governance and bargaining mechanisms convert those gains into broadly shared outcomes.

TASC’s 2026 annual inequality report, from which the AI issue brief was drawn.
Related Irish economic modelling of AI adoption, income distribution and public finances.

boundary: This record adds an Ireland-specific AI-and-inequality lens: exposure, complementarity, gender, skills, algorithmic management, ownership, worker voice and global externalisation are linked as a distributional system. It is an independent think-tank synthesis and issue brief, not a representative worker panel, causal forecast, administrative inequality series or proof that the cited exposure estimates will become realized displacement or wage outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official 21-page TASC PDF and publication page were reviewed for Ireland’s digital economy, AI exposure and complementarity estimates, gender and digital-skill differences, algorithmic management, bias, environmental/global supply-chain costs, governance and worker-voice recommendations.
